name: Augmentation mastopexy

card.summary: A combined breast lift and implant operation that raises sagging breasts and adds volume in one procedure, giving a higher, fuller breast shape.
card.aka: SAM; simultaneous augmentation mastopexy; breast lift with implants; mastopexy-augmentation
card.note: Combines two operations; pooled studies report higher complication and revision rates than either alone.

quick.overview:
Augmentation mastopexy (often abbreviated SAM) pairs a breast lift (mastopexy) with breast implants. The lift repositions the nipple and removes excess skin so the breast sits higher, and the implant adds upper-pole fullness and volume. People choose it when sagging and a wish for more volume occur together, for instance after pregnancy, weight loss or implant removal.

Surgeons describe it as one of the more technically demanding cosmetic breast operations because the implant stretches the skin while the lift tightens it. A 2014 systematic review of 23 studies pooled a 13.1 percent complication rate, with recurrent sagging the most frequent issue [1].
quick.how: The operation is performed by a plastic surgeon under anesthesia, either as one combined stage or as two staged operations. Surgeons choose a lift pattern (around the areola, vertical or anchor-shaped) according to how much the nipple has descended, then place an implant above or below the chest muscle. Recovery typically involves a surgical bra, activity limits for several weeks and scars that mature over about a year.
quick.risks: Reported risks include recurrent sagging, poor scarring, capsular contracture, asymmetry, nipple position or sensation changes, infection, hematoma, seroma and further surgery. Smoking, diabetes and obesity are associated with higher wound and nipple-blood-supply risks. Implants carry their own long-term considerations, such as rupture and the need for monitoring or replacement.

lead: Augmentation mastopexy, commonly shortened to SAM (simultaneous augmentation mastopexy), is a cosmetic breast operation that combines a mastopexy (breast lift) with breast augmentation by implant. For people whose breasts have both descended and lost volume, it aims at a higher nipple position, a tighter skin envelope and more fullness, which together give a perkier, rounder breast profile that many seek for their overall figure.[1][2]

The two goals pull in opposite directions: the implant adds volume and stretches skin, while the lift removes skin and tightens the envelope. Plastic surgery literature calls the combination among the most demanding in the field, and techniques have evolved over decades through periareolar, circumvertical and inverted-T lift patterns, along with adjuncts such as mesh, fat grafting and internal support.[2][3] Some surgeons perform both in one stage; others stage them, lifting first and augmenting later, or the reverse.

Research consists mainly of case series and reviews. A 2014 systematic review of 23 studies found a pooled complication rate of 13.1 percent, led by recurrent ptosis (5.2 percent) and poor scarring (3.7 percent).[1] Newer work looks at supportive techniques for patients with massive weight loss and at scaffold-assisted lifts.[4]

angle.text: People use augmentation mastopexy to change both the position and the volume of the breast in one operation, which alters bust projection and the proportions of the torso. It is chosen mostly by those with sagging plus reduced volume, for example after pregnancy or weight loss.

infobox: Often assessed after about a year

paras: Mastopexy addresses ptosis, the downward drift of breast tissue and nipple relative to the inframammary fold, usually graded by the Regnault classification. Augmentation adds volume with a saline or silicone implant. When both are needed, patients and surgeons can combine them in one operation or plan separate stages.[1][2]

Lift patterns range from the periareolar (donut) lift for mild descent through vertical (lollipop) lifts to the anchor or inverted-T pattern for greater descent; the more skin removed, the more scarring.[2] The choice of implant size and plane interacts with the lift, which is why planning often includes measurements such as skin stretch, nipple-to-fold distance and vertical excess.[5]

Typical candidates have sagging with loss of upper breast fullness after pregnancy, breastfeeding, weight change or ageing, or sagging remaining after implant removal. Patients with massive weight loss have lax tissue and a damaged soft-tissue envelope, and a 2024 review describes approaches such as cerclage suspension, subfascial augmentation, composite fat grafting and mesh support for this group.[4]

Published reviews describe the evolution from simple periareolar approaches toward combinations of internal support and refined skin patterns, with mesh, implants and fat grafting used as adjuncts.[2] A 2013 prospective photographic measurement study of 196 cosmetic breast cases compared how dimensions changed after augmentation, mastopexy, augmentation-mastopexy and reduction.[6]

A 'tissue-based triad' approach proposed in 2014 uses preoperative measurements of skin stretch, nipple-to-fold distance and vertical excess to plan the operation.[5] Staged and single-stage strategies are both described in the literature.

A 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis of single-stage augmentation-mastopexy included 23 studies with follow-up from 16 to 173 weeks, mostly under one year. It pooled a total complication rate of 13.1 percent; recurrent ptosis occurred in 5.2 percent, poor scarring in 3.7 percent, capsular contracture in 3.0 percent and tissue-related asymmetry in 2.9 percent, while infection, hematoma and seroma were each under 2 percent.[1] The authors described the literature as sparse and heterogeneous.[1]

A 2013 prospective study measured breast dimensions in 196 cases across augmentation, mastopexy, augmentation-mastopexy and reduction.[6] Registered trials include a completed randomized study of mastopexy with autologous augmentation after massive weight loss (22 participants) and a trial of scaffold support for recurrent ptosis (76 participants).[7][8]

Reported complications include recurrent sagging, poor scarring, capsular contracture, asymmetry, infection, hematoma and seroma.[1] Nerve injury and persistent postoperative pain after breast surgery are described in reviews of painful complications of aesthetic surgery.[9] Combined procedures also carry the implant-related considerations of rupture, replacement and monitoring discussed for breast augmentation generally.[10]

Reference descriptions of mastopexy list smoking, diabetes and obesity as factors tied to wound and nipple-blood-supply problems, and note that scars can complicate later breast imaging interpretation.[11]

General descriptions of mastopexy recovery mention a surgical bra, taped incisions, avoiding underwire bras while implants settle, and follow-up visits in the first weeks, with scar maturation and final contour taking around a year.[11]

timeline.event: Journal editorial 'Augmentation/Mastopexy: Surgeon, Beware' highlights the procedure's difficulty.[12]
Aesthetic Surgery Journal publishes an overview of augmentation mastopexy.[13]
Systematic review of single-stage augmentation-mastopexy pools complication rates.[1]
Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery continuing-education review describes the evolution of mastopexy and augmentation mastopexy techniques.[2]
Review of approaches for the nontraditional weight-loss patient.[4]
